In one run, GPT-6 Cyber helped us validate 948 Linux kernel bugs that could grant local root access and generate patches for review.

Our researchers @clintgibler and @ky1ebot share their findings and how they worked with maintainers to get fixes upstream.

Read the research:

We’re introducing Shirudo, an open-source Linux runtime allowing agents to defend systems without downtime. It lets agents write dynamic eBPF controls to shield systems from exploits, giving defenders more time to test and roll out patches. Built by @cisco together with OpenAI.

Shirudo is a first step toward self-defending infrastructure that can adapt to new threats while keeping services running. Our goal is for defenders to work with AI agents to find affected systems, test and share shields, and deploy them without disrupting workloads.

Through our new program OpenWorks, we fund local AI experts to help small businesses develop the tools and skills they need to grow their own business, at no cost to them.

We invite AI experts who love teaching others and small business owners who want to learn to implement AI to join us at
How AI is helping scientists uncover new leads for understanding and treating neurodegenerative diseases—and the brain research behind our collaboration with @perturbai_tx and @scrippsresearch:

Distillation can reproduce powerful AI capabilities without the safeguards built around them.

We’re sharing new research on our work to combat distillation of our models, how these capabilities transfer, and how we detect and disrupt coordinated attempts.

These findings are helping us sharpen our defenses and support safeguards across the industry.

MedChemBench is a new benchmark for AI reasoning in medicinal chemistry.

It shows the progress our frontier models have made in their ability to help scientists use AI to identify promising drug candidates.

We're sharing new data on how AI is changing research at OpenAI.

We find researchers' AI use continues to rise exponentially, and agents are completing longer tasks, but human involvement remains central in research. Researchers are also spending more time on safety and alignment, with human effort in these areas growing faster than in any other individual research area.

This report aims to increase transparency around research acceleration and inform the governance of increasingly capable AI. We believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI): the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems. 

Our hope is that this expanded report will help sustain and advance shared measurement norms across the industry.
We’re sharing how we approach safety at every stage of a model’s lifecycle, from early research to internal use to public deployment.

Working with @AMD, our models identified up to 14% PPA improvement on flagship GPU IP in less than five months—building on designs AMD’s engineers had already spent years optimizing.

The same approach helped improve Jalapeño, our first custom inference chip, with gains verified on real silicon.

New evaluations also show our models getting better at certain chip design tasks.

We’re sharing these results and how we’re working with @Synopsys to bring our model capabilities and their trusted EDA design and validation tools to more chip designers.

Scientists reported nearly doubling their productivity with AI in our study of more than 1,800 participants in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program.

Using privacy-preserving methods, we looked at how they use ChatGPT across their work—from developing ideas to analyzing data and writing code—and what it could mean for scientific discovery.

We’re expanding free access to our frontier models for up to 200,000 scientists worldwide, with training and support.

Applications open Nov. 23. By default, we don’t use data shared through the program to train our models.

Physicist Nathaniel Craig shares how he worked with GPT-6 Astra to develop a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model.

It’s the first post on our new science blog:

We're turning our lessons from defending OpenAI into practical tools for our customers. On Thursday, join us at Cyber at the Frontier, a live keynote, for our latest cyber announcements.

Working with our frontier models, we've identified and resolved important vulnerabilities in our own code and infrastructure. That experience is informing the tools and playbooks we're building to help other security teams strengthen their defenses.

@gdb shares what we've learned and why security teams should keep putting the latest models to work as capabilities improve.

Tune in on November 12 at 10 a.m. PT:

We built Control Room, a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.

It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our misalignment monitoring systems, and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job.

Control Room is just one part of our holistic approach for safe frontier model training and deployment.

We partnered with @fmf_org and its member firms on a new framework to help identify when bypassing an AI system's safeguards could enable serious cyber harm, and prioritize stronger protections.

"...This framework is an important step toward a common methodology for evaluating and comparing the severity of cyber jailbreaks, including the capabilities they unlock and how readily they can be used. Shared approaches like this can help the AI and security communities build a clearer evidence base and prioritize improvements to safeguards."  - OpenAI's Sasha Baker, Head of National Security Policy
